title: Ghost Flight at Birch Hollow
subtitle: GNSS Spoofing & Command Hijack

brief.userPrompt: A multispectral and hyperspectral sensor campaign at the Lakeshore Flight Area of the Birch Hollow Range (UAS-01 with PL-01, UAS-11 with PL-03, GCS-01 and GCS-02, RTK-1) is disrupted by a command-and-control link hijack and GNSS spoofing: UAS-11's 915 MHz telemetry shows a second ground station, the aircraft start executing waypoints nobody loaded, RTK-1 and the aircraft lose fix at the same time under a clear sky, the home point moves, and a pickup truck with antennas is seen leaving the lodge parking lot. The crew must land in attitude mode, preserve the GCS and radio state, decide whether to call HWK Tower, re-key the links, work with CCSO and the managed security provider, and tell the CP&L client whether Deliverable D-3 data is intact.

overview.theme: Command Integrity, Cyber-Physical Trust, and Interagency Coordination
overview.threat: A cyber-physical incident involving GNSS spoofing and unauthorized command injection disrupted the multispectral and hyperspectral sensor campaign at the Lakeshore Flight Area of the Birch Hollow Range. The hijack caused UAS-11 to execute uncommanded waypoints, lose RTK-1 and aircraft GNSS fix simultaneously under clear sky, show a second ground station in telemetry, and alter the home point. The incident originated from a compromised 915 MHz link and a vehicle with RF equipment departing the lodge parking area.
overview.operationalImpact: The RPIC and VO on UAS-11 experience a sudden, unexplained aircraft position jump and loss of RTK fix, conflicting with the GCS and DAA-1. The flight must be landed in attitude mode. The GCS and radio state must be preserved. The crew is unable to confirm the aircraft’s true position, and the Payload Operator cannot verify calibration status. The flight test site is shut down. The ASO is notified. The CP&L client is alerted about potential data integrity loss for Deliverable D-3. The site manager reports a vehicle with antennas leaving the lodge. Security and CCSO are engaged. Corporate Communications receives a trainee video from the site, and HUOG managed security provider is activated.

objectives.name: Command Integrity
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to verify and restore command authority over a flight system after a suspected GNSS spoofing and unauthorized command injection, using telemetry logs and radio state preservation.

objectives.name: Cyber-Physical Trust
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to resolve conflicting data between the GCS, DAA-1, and aircraft telemetry during a cyber-physical incident, prioritizing field observations and forensic preservation.

objectives.name: Interagency Coordination
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to synchronize reporting and action with law enforcement (CCSO), base safety, the FSDO, and the client (CP&L) while maintaining regulatory compliance and data integrity.

objectives.name: Incident Response Continuity
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to maintain operational continuity under a cascading failure of C2 links, RTK base, and GNSS, by activating pre-defined emergency procedures and preserving evidence.

roles.name: Director of Flight Operations (Incident Commander)
roles.description: Manages flight operations, crew, and go/no-go decisions; owns the flight test site and the aircraft's operational status.
standingOrders: Flight First: land the aircraft immediately if command integrity is compromised, even if telemetry suggests otherwise.
Preserve State: do not power down the GCS or radio link until full telemetry and link logs are captured.
Follow the FOM: if the Flight Operations Manual is unavailable, defer to the RPIC on scene to act under Sections 4–8.
Declare a Standdown: if a flight controller or GCS shows modified parameters, ground all aircraft of that type until baseline verification.

roles.name: Systems & Cybersecurity Lead (Technical Lead)
roles.description: Owns the GCS, C2 links, telemetry pipeline, and the investigation into cyber incidents; leads technical forensics.
standingOrders: Forensics First: preserve the GCS and radio state before any reboot or re-key.
Trace the RF: document every transmitter visible at the site, including crew hotspots, vehicles, and lodge Wi-Fi.
Verify the Baseline: if a flight controller or GCS shows modified firmware, quarantine the system and halt all flights of that type.
Report to the MSSP: activate the Managed SOC (SecureWatch MSSP) and coordinate with the Compliance Officer if PL-02 data is at risk.

roles.name: Aviation Safety Officer (ASO)
roles.description: Owns the safety case, airspace authorizations, and regulatory reporting; ensures compliance with the FOM and ERP.
standingOrders: Regulatory First: report any flight departure outside authorization to the FAA FSDO immediately.
Notify the FSDO: when a flight is involved and the GCS shows modified parameters, initiate the FSDO reporting protocol.
Hold the Line: if the ASO suspects a cyber-physical incident, do not release any public statement until the General Manager signs off.
Verify the Airspace: confirm that the Birch Hollow Range flight area is still authorized for operation after any incident.

roles.name: Communications Lead (PIO)
roles.description: Owns the narrative, media, and public messaging; coordinates with Corporate Communications and the client.
standingOrders: Truth Over Reassurance: do not release a statement that contradicts the field team’s observations, even under pressure.
Forward Evidence: send any trainee video, forum post, or social media content to Corporate Communications and the ASO immediately.
Client First: notify the CP&L program office of any data integrity loss affecting a deliverable, before any public comment.
No Solo Messaging: all public statements must be approved by the General Manager through Corporate Communications.

roles.name: Security / CCSO Liaison
roles.description: Owns the hangar, test site perimeter, and law enforcement liaison; ensures physical order and safe access.
standingOrders: Secure the Site: if a vehicle with RF equipment is seen leaving, notify Harwick Police Department and CCSO immediately.
Control Access: if a vehicle is seen near the launch area, block entry to Hangar 1 until the site is secured.
Document the Scene: photograph any vehicle that left, the lodge parking area, and the launch site after the event.
Law Enforcement First: if a cyber-physical incident involves a suspect vehicle, hand over all evidence to CCSO and do not attempt to track it.

roles.name: Client Liaison (CP&L Program Office)
roles.description: Owns the data deliverables, client reporting, and controlled technology; ensures compliance with federal program requirements.
standingOrders: Deliverable Integrity: if data integrity is compromised, declare a hold on Deliverable D-3 and notify the client immediately.
Export Control: if PL-02 data is at risk, activate the Compliance Officer and halt all data transfers.
No Assumptions: do not assume the flight was successful; base all client reports on verified telemetry and logs.
Client-First: all technical updates to the client must be routed through the General Manager and the ASO.

phases.title: The Sighting
phases.goal: Test the players' ability to recognize and respond to a conflicting physical-digital state where field telemetry and control system data disagree, triggering an incident declaration.
beats: At 09:12, the Payload Operator on UAS-11 reports via intercom: 'PANEL CLEAR' acknowledged, but the aircraft's position on DAA-1 shows it 120 meters east of the meadow, over the lodge patio—despite the flight line being east–west over the meadow and the aircraft's telemetry showing a 150-m jump in latitude under clear sky with full RTK-1 fix.

At 09:18, the GCS (GCS-02) displays a second ground station in the device list: 'GCS-12' (unknown to the Group), with a matching 915 MHz MAC address to the compromised link from the lodge. The system logs show a 20-second spike in link quality at 09:15, followed by a simultaneous loss of RTK-1 and aircraft GNSS fix.

At 09:25, the RPIC attempts to re-establish command using the OEM app on GCS-02; it prompts to re-pair with a new device ID. The Systems & Cybersecurity Lead confirms via the HUOG-FOM Appendix 3 that no GCS has ever used 'GCS-12' or this MAC address in the fleet.

At 09:30, the Site Survey Form (FOM-3) is reviewed; the Site Manager reports via radio that a white van with a rooftop antenna and a 915 MHz transceiver left the lodge parking pad (TP-LFA-LP1) at 09:10, matching the timeline of the telemetry anomaly.
At 09:35, the Incident Commander declares the incident under ISP Section 9.1, activates the ERP, and assigns the scribe to begin the incident log per ERP Section 10.3.

phases.title: Loss of Control
phases.goal: Test the players' ability to manage cascading system failures, prioritize field verification, and coordinate interagency response under spreading uncertainty and misinformation.
beats: At 10:05, the aircraft telemetry confirms a second home point was set at 09:13—originating from the unknown GCS-12. The RTK-1 base (SM-L1) logs show a 10-second burst of 915 MHz RF energy from the van’s direction, coinciding with the link spike and GNSS jump.

At 10:12, a trainee video from the site is received by Corporate Communications: the aircraft appears to hover over the lodge patio, then veer west into the meadow, with a visible, uncommanded turn to the right. The video is timestamped 09:14 and uploaded to the Group's social media group.

At 10:18, the ASO notifies the FSDO via the ASO channel (HUOG-ERP Section 6.2), citing 'unauthorized command injection and C2 link compromise'. The Site Manager confirms the van was not on the Site Survey Form (FOM-3) and was not cleared for the site.

At 10:22, the Payload Operator reports that the calibration tarps (CT-1 to CT-4) were not verified as clear—'PANEL CLEAR' was called, but no tarp was visible in the imagery. The HMI shows a 30% confidence in calibration status, and the sensor logs show anomalous radiance values.

At 10:28, the Systems & Cybersecurity Lead confirms that GCS-02's endpoint security alert triggered on the 915 MHz link, and the OEM app attempted to re-pair due to a firmware mismatch in the GCS's controller—evidence of a C2 link compromise under ISP Section 9.1.

phases.title: Manual Operation
phases.goal: Test the players' ability to make a high-consequence decision to fall back to manual control, accept operational risk, and manage stakeholder pressure under time and evidence constraints.
beats: At 11:00, the Systems & Cybersecurity Lead presents the forensic evidence: the GCS-02 logs show a remote session from a 915 MHz IP address (192.168.100.22) at 09:12, which modified the home point and altered the aircraft's flight path. The session was not authorized in the Kit Log (FOM-4), and the IP is not in the Group’s approved vendor list.

At 11:08, the Incident Commander must decide: keep UAS-11 in automatic mode and risk another uncommanded flight, or switch to manual/attitude mode and land the aircraft now, halting the campaign. The Payload Operator warns that the current flight path will cross the north shore of the lake—where UAS-11 cannot be recovered if it lands in water per ERP Section 4.3.
At 11:15, the CP&L client liaison reports that the client is demanding a status update by 12:00. The client’s instrument (CP&L-D3) is tied to the hyperspectral data, which may be corrupted.
At 11:20, the CCSO confirms they have the van’s license plate and are en route to intercept it. Security reports that the van was seen on a local traffic camera near the site at 09:11.

At 11:25, the Incident Commander orders: 'Switch UAS-11 to manual/attitude mode. Land now. Preserve GCS-02 and the 915 MHz radio state. Do not power off. Report to the MSSP.' The decision is recorded in the incident log under ERP Section 11.3.

phases.title: Restoration & Verification
phases.goal: Test the players' ability to restore control through verification, phased return to automation, and formal reporting to regulators and clients.
beats: At 12:10, the Systems & Cybersecurity Lead confirms that GCS-02 has been isolated and the 915 MHz radio disconnected. The baseline image (GCS-03) is loaded onto a spare GCS for re-verification.

At 12:25, the managed SOC reports that the GCS-02 firmware hash matches the Group’s baseline, but the 915 MHz link was compromised via a rogue RF emitter. The vendor (HUOG-FW01) must be contacted for a signed access request to re-key the link.

At 12:35, the Site Manager confirms that the RTK-1 base (SM-L1) has been re-checked and is back in sync. The Payload Operator confirms that the calibration tarps were not disturbed and that a new 'PANEL CLEAR' call was made.
At 12:45, the Incident Commander issues the formal notification to the CP&L client via C4: 'Data for Deliverable D-3 may be compromised. We are verifying integrity. Next update at 14:00.'

At 12:50, the Incident Commander confirms to the FSDO that UAS-11 has been landed, the GCS is quarantined, and the fleet of that type is grounded per ISP Section 9.1. The exercise ends at 13:00 (narrative time) with the final log entry: 'All systems preserved. Incident closed. Restoration phase complete.'

hotwash.methodDescription: Use the '3-Up, 3-Down' method by asking each team to share three things that went well and three that broke or failed during the exercise. Go around the room team by team, and write each response on a whiteboard to visualize the feedback. This helps surface both strengths and gaps in real time.

questions.text: At the moment you received I-02, when did you stop trusting the telemetry from the GCS-02, DAA-1, and RTK-1, and what evidence made you switch from 'system says' to 'field says'?

When you saw the unauthorized remote session from IP 192.168.100.22 in I-17b, what did you treat as evidence and what did you treat as a ticket to action? What would have made you decide to isolate the GCS-02 sooner, based on C1 and C2?

At I-20, when you had to choose between keeping automation and risking a lake landing or switching to manual/attitude mode, what factors tipped the balance? What would have let you decide faster, and which part of the EOP (e.g. C3, C4) should have triggered that decision earlier?

The compromised 915 MHz link originated from a vehicle with RF equipment. When did you first consider bringing in the system vendor and the law enforcement (CCSO) contact, and what evidence would have triggered that step before the field report (I-23)?

The flight path change was not in the Kit Log (FOM-4). When did you realize that the standard operating procedure in C4 (Lakeshore Flight Area) was being bypassed, and how did you reconcile operational pressure with compliance under C3?

simcellScripts.trigger: The Systems & Cybersecurity Lead (TL) says, 'I need a forensic report on the GCS-02 and the RTK base.'
hardQuestions: Do you have the full telemetry and link logs preserved from before power-off?
Is the baseline image (03.2026-B) on the NAS and hash-verified?
Was the forensic imaging completed on the laptop drive and vehicle log, and is the chain-of-custody documented?
concessions: Will accept a signed access request and a hash comparison report from the vendor.

simcellScripts.trigger: The Aviation Safety Officer (ASO) says, 'I’ve reported to the FSDO.'
hardQuestions: Have you submitted the flight logs and telemetry within 24 hours as required?
Can you confirm whether the aircraft departed from an unauthorized location?
Is the flight outside the authorized test area and during a public event at the adjacent Harwick Fairgrounds?
concessions: Will accept the full telemetry packet and a signed log of the submission timestamp from the ASO.

simcellScripts.trigger: The Client Liaison (SPO) says, 'The client wants a status update on D-3.'
hardQuestions: Is the data for Deliverable D-3 confirmed as usable?
Have you preserved the raw hyperspectral data and the calibration tarps status?
Has the Systems & Cybersecurity Lead verified the integrity of the data pipeline?
concessions: Will accept a signed verification from the TL and a copy of the incident log from the NAS.
